chapters.title: Chapter 4: India's Position in the New Trade Order

lessons.title: India's Own Vulnerabilities: Crude, Semiconductors and Capital Goods Import Dependence

children.text: The last two lessons told a story of India winning: PLI-driven electronics, resilient pharma exports, a genuine specialty chemicals tailwind. That story is real, but it is only half the picture, and a macro investor who stops there will badly misjudge India's actual exposure to the fragmenting order this course has been describing since Chapter 1. India is not just a beneficiary of other countries reducing dependence on China. India is, in several critical categories, deeply dependent itself, on crude oil, on semiconductors and, in an uncomfortable twist, on Chinese capital equipment to build the very factories powering its own China+1 success stories.

body.text: India is simultaneously a winner from global de-risking and one of the more exposed economies to the exact same fragmentation risks it is benefiting from elsewhere. Both things are true at once, and treating only the winning half as the complete story is a genuine analytical error.

children.text: Crude Oil: The Largest and Most Persistent Vulnerability

India imports roughly 85% of the crude oil it consumes, making it one of the world's largest oil importers and putting crude consistently at or near the top of India's import bill. Chapter 1 already covered how India navigated the 2022 Russia-Ukraine shock by pivoting toward discounted Urals crude, but that pivot solved a pricing problem, not the underlying dependence. India's total crude import bill has swung between roughly $130 billion and $160 billion a year depending on global oil prices, and that single number is one of the largest drivers of India's current account deficit and, through it, rupee volatility.

body.text: Diversifying suppliers, as India did with Russian crude, reduces price risk and single-country concentration risk. It does not reduce the structural vulnerability of importing 85% of a commodity whose global price India does not control. These are two different risks, and solving one does not solve the other.

children.text: Semiconductors: The Chokepoint, From India's Side

Chapter 3 examined the Taiwan chokepoint from a global perspective. From India's side, the exposure is close to total: India currently has no significant domestic chip fabrication capacity of its own. The India Semiconductor Mission, and a Tata Electronics fab under construction in Dholera, Gujarat in partnership with Taiwan's PSMC, targets mature-node chip production, not the leading-edge capacity concentrated in Taiwan, and is aimed at a production start later in this decade. Until that capacity exists and scales, every electronics success story from the previous two lessons, Apple's assembly partners, Dixon Technologies, the entire PLI-driven mobile phone export boom, is built on top of a fully imported chip supply chain.

body.text: India's semiconductor fab timelines are moving targets that shift with construction progress and policy announcements. Verify the current operational status of the India Semiconductor Mission's projects against recent primary sources rather than relying on the framing above as current.

children.text: Capital Goods: Building "Make in India" With Imported Machines

This is the least discussed and most ironic vulnerability of the three. Building new PLI-linked factories requires machine tools, industrial robotics, electrical machinery and specialised manufacturing equipment, and China remains one of India's largest suppliers of exactly this category of capital goods. As India's manufacturing investment boom has accelerated, imports of Chinese machinery and electrical equipment have often grown alongside it, not shrunk, because the factories built to reduce dependence on Chinese finished goods still need to be equipped with Chinese-made production equipment in the meantime.

The clearest single number that captures this whole tension is India's overall trade deficit with China, which government and trade research data put at roughly $85 billion in FY24, a figure that has stayed stubbornly large, and at times widened, even as the China+1 narrative around India has grown louder every year.

body.context: Remains large despite years of China+1 narrative around India, reflecting continued reliance on Chinese components, machinery and capital equipment.

markDefs.definition: A country that gains trade share from a restricted partner while itself remaining, or becoming more, dependent on that same partner for inputs, capital or intermediate goods, the exact pattern Chapter 1 identified in Vietnam and Mexico's trade data.

children.text: pattern using Vietnam and Mexico as examples: countries gaining trade share from a restricted partner while remaining, or becoming more, dependent on that same partner underneath the surface. India fits this pattern more closely than its own national narrative usually admits. It is winning assembly and export business precisely because global companies are diversifying away from China, while its own imports of Chinese machinery, components and, indirectly through the global chip market, chip-adjacent supply chains, have not meaningfully shrunk. This is not a criticism of India's strategy, every country pursuing China+1 diversification faces some version of this same tension. It is a reminder that the phrase "reducing dependence on China" needs to specify dependence on China for what, because the honest answer, for India as for Vietnam and Mexico, is usually "for some things, not all things."

body.title: Explain the paradox to a client
body.scenario: A client reads a news article celebrating India as the world's next great manufacturing hub, citing PLI-driven electronics export growth, and asks why India's trade deficit with China has not shrunk if India is genuinely reducing its dependence on China.
body.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain this apparent contradiction using the specific vulnerabilities covered in this lesson.
body.modelAnswer: India's electronics export growth is real, but it depends on imported semiconductors and components, and India's broader manufacturing investment boom requires importing Chinese capital goods and machinery to build the very factories driving that export growth. India is reducing China dependence for some finished goods while its dependence on China for machinery, components and chip-adjacent supply chains has not shrunk to match, which is exactly why the overall bilateral trade deficit has stayed large even as the export success story gets louder.

body.title: Name the pattern
body.textWithBlank: A country that gains trade share from a restricted partner while remaining dependent on that same partner for inputs or capital is called a ___, the same pattern this course has now applied to Vietnam, Mexico and India itself.
body.explanation: Chapter 1 introduced this term using Vietnam and Mexico's trade data. This lesson applies the same lens to India, showing that the pattern is not unique to smaller manufacturing hubs, it applies to any economy positioned between a dominant incumbent supplier and diversifying global demand.

cards.definition: The share of a country's crude oil consumption met through imports; roughly 85% for India, a structural vulnerability independent of which supplier countries it sources from.

Semiconductor manufacturing at older, larger-transistor process technologies, the segment India's emerging domestic fab capacity targets, as distinct from the leading-edge nodes concentrated in Taiwan.
Reliance on imported machinery, industrial equipment and production tools, which can persist or even grow during a manufacturing investment boom even as finished-goods import dependence falls.

points: India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil, and diversifying suppliers, as it did toward Russian crude after 2022, reduces price and concentration risk without reducing this underlying structural dependence.

India has essentially no domestic leading-edge or scaled mature-node chip fabrication yet, meaning its entire electronics export success story sits on top of a fully imported semiconductor supply chain.

Building PLI-driven factories requires machine tools and industrial equipment, much of it still imported from China, creating a paradox where reducing China dependence in finished goods can coincide with rising China dependence in capital equipment.
India's trade deficit with China stood at roughly $85 billion in FY24, remaining large despite years of China+1 narrative, a clear sign that dependence has shifted category rather than disappeared.

India fits the same connector-country pattern Chapter 1 identified in Vietnam and Mexico: gaining share as a diversification destination while remaining dependent on the same partner it is diversifying away from, just for different categories of goods.

Any complete assessment of India's position in the new trade order has to hold both halves of this lesson and the previous two together: real sectoral wins, and real, largely unresolved structural dependencies.
